introduction-the-multiplayer-problem.core: Collaborative and offline-first apps (documents, whiteboards, shopping lists) let many replicas edit concurrently without coordination. Conflict-free Replicated Data Types are data structures designed so concurrent updates always merge deterministically to the same result on every replica, giving strong eventual consistency without locks or central servers.

first_principles.problem: Two users edit a shared list offline, and syncing loses one person's changes.
truths: Coordination-free edits are fast and available.
Merge rules can be mathematically guaranteed.
derivation: Choose **CRDT types** matching data (counters, sets, maps, sequences).

analogy.title: Several people editing their own copy of a recipe
analogy.story: When copies are combined, clear rules decide the final version, and everyone ends up identical.
analogy.breaks: People can discuss conflicts; CRDTs resolve them automatically by rule, which may not match intent.

example.title: Offline shopping list
flow: Bob adds eggs and removes bread offline
Both see milk, eggs, no bread

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: No lost edits, no conflicts dialog.

check.q: What does 'strong eventual consistency' mean for CRDTs?
check.a: Replicas that have received the same updates are in the same state, regardless of order.

the-secret-sauce-commutativity-associati.core: A state-based CRDT's merge function must be commutative (merge(a,b) = merge(b,a)), associative (order of grouping doesn't matter) and idempotent (merging the same state twice changes nothing). Formally, states form a join semilattice and merge is the least upper bound. These properties make convergence independent of message order, duplication or delay.

first_principles.problem: A custom merge function gives different results depending on sync order.
derivation: Design merge as a **join (least upper bound)**.

analogy.title: Combining stamp collections by taking the union
analogy.story: Whatever order you merge albums in, or if you merge one twice, you get the same collection.
analogy.breaks: Stamp collections only grow; removals need extra structure (tombstones, tags).

code.text:
def merge(a, b): return max(a, b)
assert merge(3, 5) == merge(5, 3)              # commutative
assert merge(merge(1, 5), 3) == merge(1, merge(5, 3))   # associative
assert merge(5, 5) == 5                         # idempotent

check.q: Why must CRDT merge be idempotent?
check.a: Networks can deliver the same state or update more than once, and duplicates must not change the result.

the-lww-element-set-last-write-wins.core: A Last-Write-Wins element set keeps add and remove timestamps per element; an element is present if its latest add is newer than its latest remove. It's simple and compact, but relies on timestamps (clock skew can make the 'wrong' write win) and silently discards one of truly concurrent operations.

first_principles.problem: A user re-adds an item after removing it, but a replica with a fast clock keeps it removed.
derivation: Use **HLC or logical timestamps** to reduce skew.

analogy.title: A noticeboard where the most recent note wins
analogy.story: If two notes conflict, the later timestamp stays, even if someone's watch was wrong.
analogy.breaks: Noticeboards show both notes; LWW sets keep only one decision per element.

example.title: Skew problem
flow: Laptop adds 'milk' at real t=110 (its clock t=110)
Remove ts 130 > add ts 110 → milk stays removed

check.q: What's the main weakness of LWW sets?
check.a: They depend on timestamps, so clock skew and concurrent operations can produce surprising outcomes.

the-or-set-observed-remove-set.core: An Observed-Remove Set tags each add with a unique ID. A remove deletes only the tags it has observed. If another replica concurrently adds the same element with a new tag, that add survives the merge (add-wins semantics). It avoids timestamp reliance at the cost of storing tags or tombstones (optimised versions use version vectors).

first_principles.problem: Users expect an item re-added on one device to survive a concurrent remove on another.
truths: Removes should affect only what was seen.
Concurrent adds express intent to keep.
derivation: Add element with **unique tag** (replica ID + counter).
Merge = **union of adds minus removed tags**.

analogy.title: Removing only the sticky notes you've actually seen
analogy.story: If someone added a new note you hadn't seen, it stays.
analogy.breaks: Sticky notes are visible; tags are hidden metadata that grows without compaction.

example.title: Concurrent add/remove
flow: B sees a1, removes milk (removes a1)
Concurrently A adds milk again (tag a2)
Merge: a2 not removed → milk present

check.q: In an OR-Set, what happens with a concurrent add and remove of the same element?
check.a: The add wins, because the remove only deletes tags it observed, not the new tag.

the-g-counter-and-pn-counter.core: A G-Counter (grow-only) keeps one count per replica; increment your own entry, merge by element-wise max, value = sum. A PN-Counter pairs two G-Counters (increments P and decrements N) with value = sum(P) − sum(N). They give exact, coordination-free counters for likes, views and inventory deltas across replicas.

first_principles.problem: Like counts incremented on many replicas collide and lose updates when using a single shared integer.
truths: Each replica's own count only grows.
Decrements need a separate grow-only track.

analogy.title: Each cashier keeping their own tally
analogy.story: Totals are sums of all tallies; combining copies takes each cashier's highest tally.
analogy.breaks: Cashiers count physical sales; replicas can be added, growing the vector.

check.q: Why can't a PN-Counter enforce 'never below zero' by itself?
check.a: Replicas decrement independently without coordination, so concurrent decrements can overshoot.

state-based-vs-operation-based-crdts.core: State-based CRDTs (CvRDTs) send full (or delta) state and merge with a join, tolerating message loss, duplication and reordering but using more bandwidth. Operation-based CRDTs (CmRDTs) broadcast operations that must commute and require reliable, causally ordered, exactly-once delivery, which is lighter on the wire but needs a stronger transport. Delta-state CRDTs combine the strengths.

first_principles.problem: A collaborative editor syncing full document state on every keystroke saturates mobile bandwidth.
truths: Full state is robust but heavy.
Operations are light but need delivery guarantees.

analogy.title: Mailing the whole notebook versus mailing the latest edits
analogy.story: The whole notebook always works but is heavy; edits are light but must all arrive in order.
analogy.breaks: Mail can be resent; op-based CRDTs fail if an operation is lost without a reliable transport.

check.q: What delivery guarantee do operation-based CRDTs need?
check.a: Reliable, causally ordered, exactly-once delivery of operations.
